# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# A Careful Read of the Two-Year Follow-up

**Bottom line:** This is the strongest document in the set. It meets the standards the comment called for: randomisation, record-based output, hours measured from system logs, a two-year horizon and a registered mediation test. It answers both earlier overreaches fairly:
- The per-hour gain is not "entirely an artifact": it is about 8.5% at 24 months, with a confidence interval well clear of zero.
- "No sign of decay" was not warranted: the four long studies behind that claim all had the design features that inflate estimates.

Its own weak points are narrower:
- The summary compares figures measured in different ways.
- Two control offices changed their practices partway through, which affects the decay estimate.
- The meetings "confirmation" re-tests the same seven offices that generated the hypothesis.
- Two questions raised at nine months, backlog and cost in case-processing, are still unanswered.

## 1. Arithmetic

**Correct:**
- **Timesheet hours:** 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so output per hour is +9.8%.
- **Log hours:** 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so output per hour is +8.5%.
- **Halden 24-month figure:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, and 96.8 / 86.6 = 1.118, so +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares** sum to 100% (47 + 18 + 35).
- **Confidence intervals** for the per-hour estimates are symmetric on the log scale.
- **Counter-office staffing:** output per worker fell 11.4%, so restoring output needs about 1 / 0.886 ≈ 13% more staff. The stated 12% is close. A 9% rise in cost per contact implies labour is about three-quarters of cost per contact. That assumption is plausible but not stated.

**Inconsistent or loose:**
- **The summary mixes measures.** "Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" compares a timesheet-based figure with a log-based one. Like for like, the change is 12.5% to 9.8%. The summary's version happens to overstate the decline rather than flatter the result, but it should still compare like with like.
- **"About a quarter" is generous.** 12.5% to 9.8% is a 22% decline, closer to a fifth.
- **The decline is not tested.** The intervals at 9 months (+6.9 to +18.4) and 24 months (+4.6 to +15.2) overlap heavily, and no test of the difference is reported. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. Treating the decline as established is not.
- **Halden baseline hours.** The 40.3-hour baseline is the comment's average for all 27 time-tracking organisations. If it is reused for this 11-organisation subset rather than recalculated for those 11, the +11.8% is computed against the wrong baseline. The report should clarify.

## 2. What the report does well

- **Log-based hours** directly test whether timesheets miss work. They do a little: hours fell 11% on logs against 12% on timesheets. The effect on the conclusion is small.
- **The mediation analysis was registered** before the 24-month outcomes existed, with two named mediators and one outcome.
- **The counter arm's early end is reported as a result.** It now has a proper comparison: 7.3 minutes' wait against 4.0 in control offices. It also gives the first cost figure in any of the five documents (+9% per contact).
- **The Halden subset is described honestly** as "survivors twice over" and an upper bound.
- **Section 5 is fair to both earlier claims.** It concedes what the comment got right and documents why the review's duration finding could not support its conclusion.
- **Limitations are stated clearly,** including the unmeasured-confounding assumption that mediation relies on.

## 3. Control offices changed practice partway through

The "meeting audit" in two control offices is presented as a side observation. It also matters for the main estimate:

- From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut meetings, and their output per hour rose by about 4%.
- That raises the control group's average, which shrinks the measured gap between treated and control offices.
- As a rough guide, if offices are similar in size, the control average rises by about 1.2 points. That could account for roughly a third to a half of the 2.7-point decline between 9 and 24 months.

So part of the apparent fading may be the control group improving, not the treated offices declining. The report should give a sensitivity analysis that excludes those two offices, or that uses months 1–14 for control trends. This would make both the decay estimate and the 24-month gain more interpretable. Taking the contamination into account, the 24-month estimate is, if anything, conservative.

## 4. The mediation analysis: stronger than before, but not a replication

- **The same offices are re-tested.** The hypothesis came from seven treated offices at month six. The "confirmation" uses the same seven offices, observed longer. Registration at month 11 protects against choosing the analysis after seeing the 24-month data. It does not provide an independent sample. Whatever office-level traits produced the original correlation, such as a reform-minded manager, are still present. "Survives a registered test" is accurate. "Confirms" overstates it.
- **More office-months do not mean much more data.** Meetings vary mainly between offices, so the effective sample is still about 14 clusters. The small-cluster problem flagged at nine months applies here too, so the 28–66% interval is likely too narrow.
- **Meetings were not randomised.** Offices whose managers cut meetings most may have improved in other ways as well. The report acknowledges this assumption, and it is the main threat to the 47% figure.
- **The two pathways may overlap.** Fewer meetings could reduce fatigue. If so, the 47% and 18% shares are not cleanly separable, and their split depends on how the model is specified.
- **Where does the baseline meeting data come from?** The nine-month report said meeting data were collected only in month six, outside the registered plan. This report gives baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours). These were presumably reconstructed from calendar histories. The source should be stated, because the earlier paper implied no baseline existed.
- **What exactly do the logs record?** The report does not say whether "active log-in time" includes meetings. The −11% figure suggests it tracks total working time. If logs captured only time spent on cases, they would have fallen by about 5%. The definition affects how both the hours measure and the mediation result should be read.

The direction of the finding is credible: meetings matter more than fatigue. It fits my rough estimate from the nine-month data that most of the gain could come from removing meeting time. But it is one trial's units examined again, not an independent confirmation.

## 5. Unfinished business

- **Backlog and deadlines.** The nine-month report raised the risk of backlogs exceeding statutory deadlines. Twenty-four months is exactly when that would show, yet queue length and time-to-decision are still not reported. Output per FTE of −3.4% sustained for two years could mean a growing backlog.
- **Cost in case-processing.** The report costs the counter arm (+9% per contact) but not the arm that continued. Staff are paid for 37.5 hours, work about 33, and claim some overtime. Cost per case is the decision-relevant figure, and it is missing.
- **Halden attrition.** Okafor, lead author of the Halden paper, co-authors this report. It responds to the comment on novelty and meetings but not to its most serious finding: that the working paper misdescribed when and why nine organisations withdrew. That deserves a direct reply.
- **Sick days and resignations.** The sick-day figure is still not adjusted for the number of days worked. Resignations are still raw rates without confidence intervals.

## 6. The Halden follow-up

- **Survivors several times over.** Organisations had to complete the pilot, submit records, respond to this follow-up (14 of 23 did), and keep the scheme. The nine who did not respond may include further reverters. "Upper bound" is the right framing.
- **Reversion is higher than in the original pilot.** It is 3 of 14 (21%) here, against 5 of 61 (8%) in the original. The subsets differ, but this suggests the original 92% continuation rate may have overstated how lasting the change would be.
- **The summary's classification is stretched.** One reverting organisation is a marketing agency citing client deadlines. That is discretionary work, not coverage-bound work. Grouping it under "client-facing or coverage obligations" makes the dichotomy look tidier than it is. It is the first discretionary-sector reversion in the record, and it hints that hard external deadlines can act like coverage constraints.
- **No comparison group over two years.** Economic conditions, technology and staffing all changed, so the +11.8% is a before-and-after figure with all the usual caveats.

## 7. Bearing on earlier claims

- **The comment's "entirely an artifact."** This is now hard to sustain for discretionary public-sector work. The gain is 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) under the comment's own recommended standards. The comment's novelty prediction, that gains would vanish by about month ten, was based on Halden energy data rather than output, and Varden's output data do not bear it out. The comment's main methodological criticisms still stand.
- **The meta-analysis's "no decay."** This was not warranted. Varden's evidence does not, however, establish decay. The decline is not statistically tested, and it is partly confounded by the control offices' meeting audit. The honest position is modest fading, of uncertain size.
- **Halden's "sector-general."** Further undermined. The counter arm was ended, coverage-bound Halden organisations reverted, and the reversion rate in the follow-up subset is higher.
- **Halden's "fatigue is the main explanation."** Not supported. In the one registered test, fatigue explains about 18%, against about 47% for meetings.

## What this report can fairly claim

In one public employer's case-processing offices, cutting scheduled hours by 20% meant actual hours fell by about 11–12% over two years. Output per employee was slightly lower, by about 3%, with an interval that includes no change. Output per hour rose by about 8.5–10%.

- **Durability:** the gain may have faded somewhat from nine months, but it has not disappeared. Part of the apparent fading may come from control offices improving.
- **Mechanism:** a pre-registered analysis attributes about half the gain to fewer meetings and about a fifth to reduced fatigue. That rests on the same 14 offices and on untestable assumptions.
- **Coverage-bound work:** the policy was abandoned, because it would have raised cost per contact by about 9%.

## Updated state of the evidence

| Question | State after five documents |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8.5–10% at 24 months in the one randomised long-run study. About 12% in self-selected Halden survivors, which is an upper bound. Robust that the gain is above zero. |
| Actual hours cut from a 20% scheduled cut | About 11–14%. Consistent across all sources and measures. |
| Output per worker, discretionary work | About −2% to −3.5%. Intervals include zero, but the point estimates are consistently slightly negative. |
| Coverage-bound work | Output, service and cost all worsen. The Varden arm was ended and Halden reverters cluster here. Settled for practical purposes. |
| Durability | Modest fading from 9 to 24 months is possible but untested, and partly confounded. Nothing is known beyond 24 months. |
| Mechanism | Meetings plausibly explain about half; fatigue a smaller share. The evidence is one registered but non-independent test. |
| Can reorganisation alone deliver the gain? | Open. Only two uncontrolled offices bear on it. This needs a trial arm that reorganises without cutting hours. |
| Cost per unit of output | Known only for coverage work (+9%). Still unmeasured for discretionary work. |
| Backlog and deadline compliance | Not reported. |
